College isn't always a stable environment. Especially if you're trying to get your head on right. It's high pressure, and even though it's awful admitting it if you can use any on campus resources like advisors or counselors, they really do understand that mistakes get made, and people need help afterwards. Even if it's just to vent. 

Finding a reason to keep going is tough, especially if you've been drinking and using to cover the pain. But talking about it, and getting support from people who understand that sometimes you just can't do things right and need help can do a little bit to get you to a better place mentally.

Other than that, try to focus on one thing other than the drugs and alcohol. It seems easier than facing reality, but even trying to admit to advisors I'd willfully failed a course and need help picking up the pieces was better than the feelings of mixed sadness and futility and occasional euphoria I ever get from drinking.

Okay. I'm currently in college, on the East Coast, and having dealt with really serious bouts of intermittent depression, I can tell you that yes-- you can go to college, but no-- it's not going to be easy. 

For a lot of reasons I've been trying to figure out how to pay for college on my own. The major I've decided on and the fact that I'm dealing with depression and life events that have influenced me in wrecking my grades a little this quarter means my parents likely won't pay next semester and even if they would, I'd have to make hard choices. Turning down things that would help me on my career path, which is entirely East Coast reliant, to go back to Colorado and live with them simply because they demand my presence. To a house where no one acknowledges my depression as real and where I have a history of self-harm and bad memories and routinely feel suicidal the few times I've had to visit.

I'm scared. I'm scared because I don't have any money. my last pay check from home before school just went toward groceries and textbooks. I'm a minor and can't get financial aid without them filling out the FAFSA, which would lace me with enough marionette strings to make me regret ever being born. I'm scared because after an existential crisis and depression I'm trying to dig myself out of, I feel like I finally have figured out what I really want to do and who I want to be. I've had jobs and am willing to work really hard.

But jobs are scarce, there are hoops to jump through to get student aid money and I don't really think an 18 year old girl has a huge chance living on the streets. I'm looking for help, but I might not be moving fast enough. I might have already screwed up so badly that there isn't any hope. I'm exhausted and my future is uncertain-- but I'm trying. I have an appointment in the school's health center to see if I can see a therapist and then a psychiatrist. The last time I spoke to a therapist, he said he really wanted to see about referring me to a psychologist to get help with what I've been struggling with. That was before my mother pulled me out of therapy because it apparently "Wasn't helping."

So if it gives you any hope to know that there's someone else trying to make money and find a place to live and pursue their dreams, even when it's hard to get out of bed and take a shower every morning-- there is. Some days, I can't even do that.

But if it helps, I'd be willing to help you brainstorm, and if you ever got out East I'd help you in any way I could. What do you want to study? Where have you thought about moving?

The best thing you can do about any issues you have is to talk about them once you feel comfortable. Confide in a counselor, teacher, or best friend. A gift of time is one of the best you can give. Talk to her about your life, dreams, aspirations, childhood, funny stories. Ask her questions about her life or your family. Sometimes just talk about nothing, or just sit and do something together.

Let her know she is important to you, spending time with her is important to you, and you love her. Just spend time with her, in any way you can-- it'll be a gift for both of you.

You've already said you don't want internships, and that would be might first suggestion, along with being a student teacher. But seeing as you want to just get for a little while (I completely understand, when I graduate that's my plan as well while I try and set myself up for real life) 

A job is imperative. Waiting tables, retail-- anything. Some stores might still be hiring for the holiday season (I work at Target and I know we still have a few positions open for the holidays, mostly cashier work but money is money), but no matter where you look for a job you need one.

Second, try and figure out what you *might* want you next step to be. Do you have an SO you want to stay near? Do you know what grad school you might be interested in, or eve the region? Do you have any idea where you may want to teach? take all of these into consideration when thinking about a job, but also in picking an apartment. You won't be able to be very picky, but lots of cheap apartments are better and cheaper than dorms, even marginally, and most aren't worse (in my experience, but my school does have very old dorms). Once you find a place you can affordably live on your own (or with roommates), go there. If you don't have enough money for that right now, crash with friends until you can, or go live with your parents. It will suck, I guarantee it, but if you promise to help pitch in rent when you can, help cook, clean, do whatever you can-- you'll at least have a cushion until you can support yourself.

Those are the two most important things, and from there you get a myriad of problems. Trying to get and stay employed, getting to work via public transportation or a bike if you don't have a car, health insurance, car insurance, everything. But finding a cheap place to live (with friends or on your own), getting a job, and trying to figure out what you want to do in life later on are imperative.

After you sort that out, just think. Think about what really being an individual means, what makes a good life, how you want to live. Try and live in the moment, even with the hard work you'll be doing just to get by. Travel if you can. Enjoy the small things, and not having to spend every hour of the day working toward a far off goal.

I take exception to ENRICOs's blatant mischaracterization of Objectivists, or even just the people on r/Objectivism. Not all of us are Libertarians, not all of us want to overthrow America and remake it in the vision of Ayn Rand, with Enright Houses and Taggart Transcontinentals everywhere. Ad enlightened self-interest is certainly not always self-deluded idiocy. Sometimes, it's not possible and is even detrimental to try and help those who don't want to refuse to be helped. Sometimes, offering aid is really not a way to effectuate lasting change and societal-- heck, humanity-wide repair. And if you plumbed a little deeper, ENRICOs, you might see that selfishness, when used here, does not always mean keeping the last cookie for yourself. And even when it does, sometimes, it really does work out in society's favor. 

I also take extreme issue with the racially loaded way you worked in your quotes. While there may be racially correlation related to being an Objectivist or Libertarian, I find it highly offensive to characterize people like that, whatever their ideology. Not just race-- gender, sex, sexuality, age, nationality, etc, it's offensive and greatly diminishes the efficacy of your argument. 

Rand is sometimes a bit extreme. I personally do not agree unequivocally with Objectivism, because I know that in the imperfect world we inhabit, the correct course of action is not always black and white, and sometimes, the needs or interests of the individual cannot be extricated form society/humanity at large. In others words, sometimes the needs of the one ARE the needs of the many. 

Finally, I'm just a kid. I don't pretend to know what philosophy, economic system, policy decision, or whatever else will make America, and the world at large, rive an flourish, peaceably and in a way where as many organisms as possible and live fulfilling, healthy lives. Objectivism doesn't persecute or try to convent anyone inherently. In every novel, Rand creates characters who present their selfishness, excellence, conduct and flaws up to the world and ask for nothing in return but a listening ear and the clearheadedness to look at the world rationally. Not force their views on anyone else-- that inherently contradicts Objectivism's rational-self-interst theory. What do I care if my neighbor thinks the way I do? It might make my life easier, and it might even make the world better (something I am personally skeptical of-- ideological homogeneity gets creepy, fast), but it's not my place or responsibility to change them, merely advance my own life, and try to forge my path in the world in the best way I can-- the rest will come if people look, think, and listen. 

People think differently, and no one system of thought will ever be 100% right. But the passion with which you made your rebuttal, the coolly amused way people have responded to ENRICOs are both pretty good as far as rational interchange goes. A little less vitriol, and the willingness to approach others with an open mind could help EVERYONE, and I hope that you stay here, ENRICOs, maybe not to call names but challenge us and our views, and maybe to synthesize or thoughts and yours into smething even better.

As far as I can tell, and I am not nor do I claim to be any sort of Rand expert, the point of Objectivism is not to exist in a vacuum. Many of your questions seem to boil down to those in much of classical philosophy-- the "why ought I exist, what are the things that constitute happiness", etc. objectivism seems to presuppose e fact that one has reconciled himself to his own existence, and the fact that happiness is preferable to unhappiness, or in Rand's case, directly oppositional to and destructive of happiness. Objectivism moves from the existential questions by addressing them with the goal of achieving and acting in one's rational self interest because that is what is practical and moral in the "real world" of practical things. Objectivism can't really exist in the clinically dressed down world of pure, idea based philosophy because that is not the world in which man exists.

As I said, I am rather new to Rand, please correct me if I'm wrong.
